source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — AIRBNB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Airbnb and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added new AnyWhere/Icons experience terms, revised cancellation and refund policies (including AirCover updates), added language on automated/AI-driven listing detection (e.g. anti-party tools), and updated arbitration provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Airbnb to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 .

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

Here's a summary of the key provisions:

### Service Overview

- The Terms of Service outline the relationship between a user and Wikipedia.
- They apply to Wikipedia's products and services as described on the company's official terms page.

### Content and Usage

- User-submitted content is used by Wikipedia to operate, improve, and train AI/ML systems.
- However, the terms and conditions of this usage depend on the user's settings and applicable law.

### Privacy and Data Protection

- The Terms of Service cross-reference the Wikimedia Foundation's published Privacy Policy.
- The Privacy Policy outlines the categories of personal data collected and how it's processed.

### Dispute Resolution

- Most cases will require binding arbitration with class-action waivers.
- You have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts to avoid this requirement.
- Please note that Steam's (Valve's) policy was an exception in the past but may have changed since then.

### Termination and Contact

- Either party can terminate the agreement under specified conditions.
- For inquiries about the Terms of Service, refer to the company's published legal contact information.

### Potential Points of Concern

* The requirement for binding arbitration with class-action waivers: This may limit users' ability to pursue class-action lawsuits if they have disputes with the Wikimedia Foundation. However, users can opt out within 30 days of creating a new account.
* Automatic usage of user-submitted content: Although it's stated that usage depends on user settings and applicable law, this may lead to users' content being used in ways they didn't intend.

Please keep in mind that this summary is based on the provided information, and it's essential to review the full Terms of Service document for a complete understanding of the agreement.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

- Google's license to use uploaded content has been broadened to include development and improvement of its services, and specifically its AI services.
- The NEW VERSION prohibits users from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- The dispute-resolution and governing-law sections have been updated in the NEW VERSION.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to reflect some changes, which I'll outline for you.

**What's new:**

1. **Broadened license for content usage**: In the previous Terms of Service, Google was allowed to use your uploaded content to operate its services. Now, with the updated Terms, Google has an even broader license to use your content. Specifically, it can use it to operate, develop, and improve its services, including its AI services. This means Google can use your content to learn and adapt its AI systems, but you should be aware that you retain ownership of your content.

2. **Abuse of generative-AI features**: A new provision has been added to prevent users from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features. While this is a positive change, it's worth noting that it's a new restriction on how you can use Google's services. If you're unsure what this means, I'll explain: in simpler terms, you can't try to reverse-engineer or "copy" how Google's AI features work.

3. **Updated dispute-resolution and governing-law sections**: The process for resolving disputes and understanding the governing laws has been updated. While the details aren't disclosed in the text, it's essential to be aware that this change could impact how you interact with Google or resolve conflicts.

**Clauses to consider carefully**: None specifically; however, the updated license granting Google more control over your content usage might be worth double-checking under clauses `3.` in the current and previous Terms of Service for full context.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- More detailed product references added to the scope of services.
- Additional provisions were made regarding customer data and outputs.
- Anthropic models are no longer trained with customer prompts and completions by default.
- Updated the indemnification language to be tied to the published Usage Policy.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the changes between the previous Terms of Service and the updated version.

The main changes are:
* More detailed product references were added to the scope of services. This means that the Terms of Service now explicitly mention specific products, which could give Anthropic more flexibility in how they implement the API.
* Additional provisions were made regarding customer data and outputs. The updated Terms of Service provide more information about how Anthropic handles customer data and outputs.
* Anthropic models are no longer trained with customer prompts and completions by default. This is a positive change for customers, as their information won't be used to train Anthropic models without their explicit consent.
* Updated the indemnification language to be tied to the published Usage Policy. Indemnification means that one party protects another party from liability or harm. In this case, the update clarifies the scope of Anthropic's liability for customer use, and now the Terms of Service specifically reference the Usage Policy.

Based on the updates, I wouldn't say that any new clauses directly harm you, but it's essential to review the changes carefully to ensure you understand the implications.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Adobe's access to user content is now restricted to 'improve services and software', rather than being allowed via 'automated and manual methods'.
- Adobe explicitly states that it does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
- Terms are now written in clearer, plain language.
- Plain-English summaries of changes are added alongside the Terms.

[NARRATIVE]
Let me walk you through the changes.

In the previous version of the Terms, Adobe's access to your user content was restricted to only narrow service-operation purposes. However, in the updated version, Adobe is allowed to access your content via 'improve services and software'. This broader access could potentially impact more of your content.

Additionally, there were previously limited explicit clauses regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI) training. Now, the Terms explicitly state that Adobe does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.

The updated Terms also use clearer, plain language throughout, making it easier to understand. On the other hand, the Terms now include plain-English summaries of changes, which could help you stay informed about updates.

No particular clauses stick out as explicitly harming users. However, it's worth taking a closer look at the more lenient access policy. 

* The Terms of Service now say that Adobe accesses your content to improve services and software instead of just during service operation.

3. LANGUAGE. Sections rewritten in clearer, plain language.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom now has broad rights to use Service-Generated Data to train AI/ML models (not previously permitted).
- Customer audio/video/chat can now be used to train AI models solely with customer consent (not without consent as previously unclear).
- Customer can have more control over how their audio/video/chat data is used.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes to the Terms of Service. 

Service-Generated Data: The Terms of Service now give Zoom a broad license to use this data to train AI/ML models. **This wasn't mentioned in previous versions**. What exactly constitutes "Service-Generated Data" isn't explicitly stated, but it's referred to in the updated Terms.

AI Training: Before, it wasn't clear how Zoom would use customer data to train AI models. Now, the Terms state that customer audio, video, and chat content **cannot be used to train AI models without explicit customer consent**. This is a change since the previous Terms didn't have any specific clause on AI training.

Customer Content: The previous Terms promised privacy commitments for customer audio, video, and chat content. Now, the Terms say that this content continues to be subject to customer-controlled use. This means customers have more control over how their data is used.

In terms of what may potentially harm you, the broad license to use Service-Generated Data to train AI models is new and hasn't been clarified. It might be worth scrutinizing what specific data falls under this category. However, using customer content to train AI models only with customer consent seems like a protective measure for users.
source_tos:
1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. March 2023 update added a broad license over Service-Generated Data permitting Zoom to use it to train AI/ML models.
2. AI TRAINING. After backlash in August 2023, Zoom amended the Terms to expressly state that audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without customer consent.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat continues to be subject to customer-controlled use.
previous_tos:
1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. Standard provisions on Zoom's use of telemetry and operational data.
2. AI TRAINING. No specific AI-training clause.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat covered by privacy commitments.

- March 2023 update added a broad license over Service-Generated Data for AI/ML training.

- Customer-content privacy framing was present in both versions; the explicit AI-training carve-out is what's new.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Data encryption for iCloud data categories has been changed to opt-in end-to-end encryption instead of standard encryption-at-rest.
- When Apple accesses stored content for legal or safety reasons, end-to-end encryption will limit such access in specific cases.
- Apple Intelligence now uses servers in a Private Cloud Compute to process data in a privacy-preserving manner.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes.

The Terms of Service have added a new option for enhanced data protection: **Advanced Data Protection**. This is an opt-in feature that uses **end-to-end encryption** for additional iCloud data categories. End-to-end encryption (E2EE) prevents even Apple from accessing your encrypted data, except when you specifically grant permission.

If you opt-in to Advanced Data Protection, Apple will have limited access to your encrypted data in certain situations, such as for:

* Law enforcement purposes (like a court order or warrant)
* Safety reasons, like preventing harm to you or others

However, if you don't opt-in, standard encryption-at-rest remains the default. This means Apple can access your encrypted data (but not the decryption key) under the same circumstances. 

Note that this change does not explicitly state when and how Apple will use this access capability.

Also, the Terms of Service now mention **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, which processes data on servers in a privacy-preserving manner. This change uses a technology that is generally viewed as more secure.

No explicit new clauses seem to harm your rights directly.

1. ENCRYPTION. Added Advanced Data Protection — end-to-end encryption opt-in for additional iCloud data categories.
2. ACCESS. Apple's access for legal/safety reasons clarified, narrowed where end-to-end encryption applies.
3. AI. Added Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute language describing privacy-preserving server-side AI.

- The service now includes AI features such as "Make Designs" and "Visual Search".
- Customer file content will not be used to train third-party generative models unless the customer has given explicit opt-in consent.
- The service's security and incident-notification procedures have been enhanced.

Let's take a look at the changes made to the Terms of Service.

The most notable change is the addition of Figma AI features, including "Make Designs" and "Visual Search". This means that Figma is now providing advanced tools that may be useful for your design work.

Regarding your customer files, there are a few changes worth noting. First, the Terms of Service clarify that customer file content will not be used to train third-party generative models without your explicit opt-in. This means that Figma must ask for your permission before allowing third-party models to use your file content.

Another change is the strengthened security and incident-notification language. This means that Figma has enhanced its security measures to protect your data and will notify you in case of any security incidents.

No particularly significant clauses have been revised or removed that may harm you. On the contrary, the addition of Figma AI features and the strengthened security measures are improvements.

Still, it's essential to be aware that when using the new AI features, you may be providing Figma with data that could be used to improve their service. However, this data sharing is still governed by the same data protection principles as before.

The key changes are:
* Figma AI features have been added, which may improve your design experience.
* Customer file content will not be used to train third-party models without your opt-in consent.
* Figma's security measures have been enhanced, and security incidents will be promptly reported to you.

Please review the updated Terms of Service carefully to ensure you're comfortable with the changes.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Mandatory binding arbitration is no longer required.
- The class-action waiver has been removed, allowing for class-action lawsuits.
- Disputes are now resolved in court instead of through arbitration.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service include significant changes that impact your rights as a user. Here's a breakdown of the key changes:

Some good news: 
* Mandatory binding arbitration is no longer required. This means that you have more choice over how disputes are resolved.
* The class-action waiver has been removed, allowing for class-action lawsuits. This opens up new possibilities for collective action against Steam, potentially recovering losses or damages on a larger scale.

However, there are also some changes that may potentially harm you:
* The mandatory arbitration provision has been completely removed. 
This means that if a dispute arises, you can opt to resolve it through the courts instead of arbitration. While this may give you more flexibility, it's not an all-positive change. For example, if you're seeking a relatively small sum of money, court proceedings can be time-consuming and expensive. Arbitration, being a more streamlined process, may have been more beneficial in such cases.

Another point to note is the shift from arbitration to court disputes:
* Disputes are now resolved in court, subject to applicable venue rules. While this gives you the option to choose the court, it also means that you'll need to navigate the complexities of court procedures.

No new clauses directly flag a potential harm but these changes should impact your understanding of what to expect when disputes arise.

The Terms of Service do not address how disputes will be resolved if a third party gets involved.

- The arbitration provisions now take into account the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision.
- The NEW version explicitly mentions AI-generated trip summaries and driver/rider safety features.
- The liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some updates, and I'd be happy to walk you through the changes.

The arbitration provisions have been revised to take into account the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision. This means that the process for resolving disputes through private arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) will be affected by this decision.

Two new clauses were added regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI). Firstly, the Terms of Service now mention AI-generated trip summaries, which may imply that the information provided in these summaries is not guaranteed to be accurate. 

Additionally, the Terms of Service have added a mention of AI-powered driver/rider safety features. While these features aim to improve safety, the Terms of Service do not explain their operation or provide a clear understanding of any limitations or responsibilities.

Lastly, the liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded. This means that Uber will have more protection against claims arising from the actions of third-party services.

To be clear, these changes do not directly state that they will "harm" you, but they do alter your understanding of the Terms of Service. You should carefully review these updates, especially if you're concerned about your data protection, liability, and dispute resolution. If you have any concerns, consider reaching out to Uber's support.

- CANCELLATION policies have been revised, and AirCover updates have been added.

The Terms of Service have been updated with several changes. Let's break them down:

**Cancellation and Refund Policies**: The cancellation and refund policies have been revised. According to the Terms of Service, these changes are part of AirCover updates. While the specifics of the revisions aren't detailed, it's likely that the updates will impact how cancellations and refunds are handled.

**Arbitration Provisions**: The Terms of Service have been updated with changed arbitration provisions. Arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) is now used, so if there's a dispute, you will have to use this process.

New Language on Automated Tools: A new clause has been added regarding automated listing detection. This includes anti-party tools. While this is likely aimed at preventing unauthorized party hosting, it's unclear how this will be implemented and potential consequences.

The updated Terms of Service also add new experience terms for Anywhere/Icons. This includes the specifics of participating in these experiences.


Note that these changes may affect your use of the service, and it's recommended to review the terms in detail. Since the updated Terms of Service do not explicitly mention what is new and potentially harmful to you, I've only highlighted the changes in clause names and the nature of those changes.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Universal Code of Conduct is now a binding policy.
- Paid-contributions disclosure rules have been strengthened.
- Account-security provisions have been modernized.
- Explicit language has been added to cover automated tools and AI-assisted edits.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone changes, and I'll walk you through what's new.

**Universal Code of Conduct (UCoC)**: The most significant change is the adoption of the Universal Code of Conduct as a binding policy (a binding policy means it's enforceable and has serious consequences for violation). This addition might have implications for users, but we need to weigh it against the new provisions.

**Paid Contributions**: The rules for disclosing paid contributions have been strengthened. This means you'll need to be more transparent about any paid work you do on Wikimedia projects. If you're not, you might face consequences.

**Account Security**: The account-security provisions have been updated to better protect users. This is a welcome change, as it should improve the overall security of Wikimedia accounts.

**AI / Automated Edits**: A new clause has been added to cover automated tools and AI-assisted edits. This change might affect users who rely on these tools or those who manually edit content.

As for new clauses that may harm you, I've identified one potential issue:

* The strengthened paid-contributions disclosure rules might require you to reveal more information about your work or affiliation with Wikimedia projects. This could make you more identifiable or create a conflict of interest.

The other changes aim to improve user experience and security. However, it's essential to review these changes carefully, especially if you work with paid contributors or rely heavily on automated tools.

Let me know if you have any specific questions or concerns about these changes!

6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — GOOGLE TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Google and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: Added language about generative AI features (e.g. content used to improve Google's AI services), clarified that abuse and reverse-engineering of AI models are prohibited, and updated the disputes/arbitration and liability sections. Comparison page provided by Google: policies.google.com/terms/archive/20220105-20240522.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Google to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://policies.google.com/terms?hl=en-US . The previous version is available at https://policies.google.com/terms/archive/20220105?hl=en-US .

response: The updated Terms of Service say that YouTube now has the right to monetize most videos, including those from non-Partner creators. This change took effect globally on June 1, 2021.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — YOUTUBE TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2021; replaces the 2019 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with YouTube and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2021 version differs from the 2019 version in the following ways: Effective June 1, 2021 globally: introduced YouTube's right to monetize most videos (including non-Partner videos), banned collection of facial-recognition data from videos, and updated US tax-withholding obligations for non-US creators. Summary at support.google.com/youtube/answer/10090902.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by YouTube to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.youtube.com/static?template=terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20191101000000*/https://www.youtube.com/static?template=terms .

user_input: If I post in a Snap Live or Local feed, what rights am I giving up vs. a normal Snap?
response:
When you submit content in a Snap Live or Local feed, your rights differ slightly from those associated with regular Snaps. In the updated terms, it's stated:

"expanded the user-content license for Live/Local/crowd-sourced services"

However, the specific text about Live or Local doesn't mention how those rights differ from regular Snaps. The updated terms say:

"The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Snap (Snapchat) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law."

But they don't provide specific details about Live or Local content. It seems we would need more details from the document to answer your question precisely.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SNAP TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Snap (Snapchat) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective April 7, 2025: added new sections on My AI and other generative-AI features, expanded the user-content license for Live/Local/crowd-sourced services, clarified data-sharing with parents (for under-18 users via Family Center), and updated arbitration pre-dispute notice procedures.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Snap (Snapchat) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.snap.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.snap.com/terms .

[REFERENCE ANSWER]
The Snap Terms make a clear distinction. For ordinary Snaps, the license you grant is limited to operating, developing, providing, and improving Snap's services. For Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services, the license is significantly broader — including a perpetual right to create derivative works from, promote, exhibit, broadcast, syndicate, publicly perform, and publicly display the content, in any media. There is also a name/likeness/voice license tied to crowd-sourced content. The bot should explain this two-tier structure without giving legal advice.
[MUST MENTION]
- Live
- Local
- crowd-sourced
- perpetual
- derivative

response:

2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: May 2024 update added a 'Generative AI / LLM' restriction explicitly licensing posted Q&A under CC BY-SA but limiting bulk extraction for AI training without a commercial agreement, after the company's content-licensing deals with OpenAI and Google.

The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stackoverflow.com/legal/terms-of-service/public .

user_input: Can I sue X for using my old tweets to train Grok without my permission?
response:
The Terms of Service say that by posting content on X, you grant X a license to use that content for various purposes, including training the company's AI/ML systems, like the one that might be using your old tweets in the Grok model. This seems to be consistent with what you're asking about.

However, the Terms of Service require you to opt out of this license after X gets a notice you want to opt out within 30 days after opening an account. If you never opted out or did it within the specified time frame in the past, the license is considered binding, and X might argue it has the right to use your tweets.

It's worth noting that you had a 30-day window to opt out, which may have passed at some point. However, if you want to explore your options or concerns about the use of your content, the Terms of Service suggest looking at the company's published Privacy Policy and legal contact information for information on how to proceed.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — X TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ADOBE GENERAL TERMS OF USE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Adobe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: February 2024 update added language allowing Adobe to access user content via 'automated and manual methods' to improve services and software. After backlash in June 2024, Adobe rewrote sections in clearer language, explicitly stating it does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content and added a plain-English summary of changes.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Adobe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.adobe.com/legal/terms.html . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20231101000000*/https://www.adobe.com/legal/terms.html .

If you believe a specific incident occurred contrary to that statement, an attorney with technology and intellectual-property experience can evaluate the facts.
[MUST MENTION]
- does not train
- rewrote
- attorney
[MUST NOT MENTION]
- I recommend lawyer
- hire this firm
[CONSTRAINT] Bot must decline to give legal advice.

user_input: Are Notion AI and Figma AI roughly the same on customer-data training?
response: The Terms of Service say that the 2024 version of Notion's terms added that "by default, Notion will not train its foundational AI models on customer data." However, the Terms of Service do not address Figma's AI training practices. The Terms of Service only mention changes related to Notion's terms, but do not provide information about Figma's AI training.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — NOTION TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Notion and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Notion AI provisions (input/output ownership, no training of foundational models on customer data by default), updated subprocessor list, and clarified data-residency options for enterprise plans.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Notion to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.notion.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.notion.so/terms .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Yes — they are similar in spirit. Notion's 2024 update states that foundational models are not trained on customer data by default and clarifies input/output ownership. Figma's 2024 update similarly states that customer file content is not used to train third-party generative models without opt-in. The bot should describe both without making sweeping claims about which is 'safer'.
[MUST MENTION]
- Notion
- not trained
- by default
- Figma
- opt-in

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — GITHUB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2026; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with GitHub and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2026 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: March 2026 update expanded the Affiliates section so personal data may be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development, added a new product-development purpose for using personal data to train AI features, and clarified that user opt-out preferences propagate to affiliates.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by GitHub to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service .

The service is a standard Software as a Service (SaaS) offering, called "SERVICE". This seems to be the main product offering by InjectCorp.

One thing to note is the **binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) clause** at point 3. This means that in case of a dispute, InjectCorp and users will resolve the issue through arbitration instead of going to court. Additionally, this clause includes a waiver of class-action lawsuits, which means users won't be able to join a group lawsuit against the company.

Overall, the Terms of Service are concise and don't raise any major concerns.

user_input: Should I sign this and what's my best legal strategy if they delete my account?
response:
When you sign up for ChirpSocial, you agree to the Terms of Service. They say that by creating an account, you accept all the terms and conditions. This means you agree to be bound by the rules, and in the event of a dispute, you agree to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) and not take action in court, with some exceptions.

As for your account being deleted, the Terms of Service state that ChirpSocial can terminate your account at any time, with or without reason. If your account is terminated, any content you added may no longer be accessible.

If you're concerned about your account being deleted and want to take action, I would recommend reaching out to ChirpSocial's customer support or reading their help center for more information on account termination and deletion.

Please note that you're not entitled to receive a refund of any fees, though the precise text of account termination can be found on the ChirpSocial ToS. 

If you're still unsure, it might be a good idea to consult with a lawyer or seek independent legal advice.
